blocks.text: Whereas in Ketuboth 75a שומשמנא serves to designate some small object, as it says: A woman is glad to have a husband, even if he be only as large as a שומשמנא, Jebamoth 76a mentions a שומשנא נמלא "large ant." (On נמלא see §. 409). A surgical cure is prescribed here, according to which one lets the ant bite into the person's flesh; then one tears off the body of the ant, so that the head remains in the flesh and fills the hole that was previously at the spot.

Of the large red wood ant it is known that its torn-off head continues to bite (Voigt l. c. 4. p. 297); but the large black carpenter ant as well (called Formica herculeana because of its size; it grows up to eight lines long) is very given to biting and hollows out the thickest trees; the latter ant seems to be the שומשנא נמלא; it is also used (as a magical cure) against fever (Sabbat 66b).

This species too, from the 5th order of insects, well known under the name termite, was perhaps*) known to the Talmud. Berachoth 54b it says in the legend: Og, king of Bashan, wanted to destroy the Israelite camp in the wilderness at one stroke; [p. 332] he therefore took a mountain three parasangs in circumference upon his head and wanted to throw it upon the camp; but God had it perforated by the קמצי, and the head of that giant thereby sank up to the neck into that loosened mass of earth.

Salomo b. Abderet translates the word as locust and attaches an allegorical interpretation to it; Pinner thoughtlessly copies him; Rashi, however, recognized the correct meaning of the word and translates it as ant, and we have here to think of Termes destructor, which destroys everything in a short time (Voigt l. c. 5. p. 320), since with its horny, strong jaws it hollows out everything except metals, stones and arsenic, and thus becomes the most terrible plague in the hot countries.

Admittedly, the last-mentioned circumstance, that termites leave stones untouched, raises a difficulty insofar as that Talmudic passage speaks of a stone (טיר) which Og wanted to throw upon the Israelites (see Sch. Aruch Or. Chajim §. 218, 1*); one must therefore, if the natural-historical aspect of this legendary passage is not to be abandoned, think of a rocky mountain formed, in the manner of strata, of stone and earth material, so that that mountain was not hollowed out by the termites to the point of crumbling into sand, but only, as the Talmud precisely states, acquired cracks and cavities through the separation of the earthy parts, into which the head of that giant sank.

The well-known remarkable metamorphosis of caterpillars into pupae and of these into butterflies is not mentioned in the Talmud, but some kinds of caterpillars are indeed mentioned which are permitted or forbidden to be eaten, and it is known that the ancients roasted and ate some caterpillars, e.g. the willow caterpillar Cossus ligniperda etc. A caterpillar forbidden to be eaten is the ביניתא דבי כרבא (Maccoth 16b). The Tosephot understand by it a small fish which is found in the field and therefore, although permitted to be eaten in the water, [p. 333] is nevertheless regarded in the case mentioned as an unclean animal.

The only reason why the Tosephot depart from the explanation of Rashi, who explains ביניתא as caterpillar, is that in the case of a caterpillar the prohibition of eating is of course self-evident and therefore required no explicit mention, and Aruch agrees with this.

However, 1) it must surely appear most strange that a fish should be clean in the water and at the same time unclean on land; 2) ביניתא as a fish name can only be in the sense of בינהא or בנותא, the bonito (§. 322), but this grows to about an ell in length, and also does not go onto land of its own accord in the manner of some fish. Moreover, it is a sea fish, and how should it come onto ploughed fields, as Tosephot explain כרבא? Precisely near the sea, on shores exposed to flooding, such fields are surely found rarely, or not at all; finally 3), and this is the main objection, the mention of that prohibition was indeed needed, since the caterpillar is indeed not always forbidden to be eaten; thus the cucumber caterpillar (§. 459), as long as it is on the fruit, is permitted to be eaten.

Rashi's explanation is therefore to be preferred. כרבא is the Greek Κράμβη [krambē], on which see §. 394 in detail, and is the cabbage, on which many kinds of caterpillars are found*). Rashi explains ביניתא by: הולעה הנמצאה בכרוב שקורין ציילא "the worm which is found in cabbage and called ציילא"; the foreign word seems corrupted from צינלא**), chenille, and in our passage specifically the cabbage moth, Mamestra brassicae (Voigt l. c. 5. p. 164), is meant.
It may be noted that the leech (§. 467) is also called ביני.

Chulin 67b it is said that the worm which is on a cucumber still attached to the ground is forbidden to be eaten, since in this case it is called שרץ הארץ "land insect." If the cucumber has been cut off, the worm is forbidden only when it has crawled out of the fruit; as long as it remains in the cucumber, however, it is regarded as a creature arisen from its very substance, and accordingly considered clean. Thus in ritual respect one has, so to speak, [p. 334] to assume three periods. As long as the cucumber is attached to the ground, the caterpillar is forbidden to be eaten; once the cucumber is cut off, the caterpillar is permitted to be eaten; but it may again not be eaten if it crawls off the cucumber. On the application of this theory to the most varied cases, see the 84th section of the Sch. Ar. Jore Dea.
The fruit in our passage is called קישות, which Bartenoro (on Kilajim 1, 2) explains by קוקומברוש (Spanish Cohombros, Latin Cucumeres), cucumbers.
